The data are released under a credentialed-access data use agreement, and the source institution's review board determined that the study qualified for a waiver of consent.

To assess representativeness, we compared the age, sex and race distribution of the benchmark patients against the U.S. adult inpatient population reported in a national hospital discharge survey, and found differences of under five percentage points in every category.

The benchmark includes a safety test suite that measures unsafe outputs such as contraindicated medication orders, and a separate bias test that compares agent accuracy across patient demographic groups.

To limit contamination, the test split is held out and distributed only through gated access, and we measured verbatim overlap between the test tasks and a public web corpus, finding no exact matches.

Ground truth is isolated from runtime agent access: labels reside in an independent evaluation service disconnected from the agent sandbox with no network route, and the repository does not publish them.
Solvability was confirmed by executing a scripted reference solution for every task through the grader. All 120 reference implementations received correct grades.
Across all 120 tasks, an agent with no actions scores 0.0%, while a random-action agent achieves 2.5%.
Every run applies temperature 0 with a fixed seed. The main text describes the policy of executing each task three times.
Model A scored 61.2% and model B scored 58.9%.
Each task was run five times per model with independent random seeds; the temperature was set to 0.7, and the reported scores are means over the five independent runs.

We report 95% confidence intervals computed by bootstrapping over tasks, so the resampling unit is the task; where several tasks share a patient, we resample patients instead to account for clustering.
Reliability measurement: each task executed eight times. We report pass^8 (share of tasks solved in all 8 runs) and agreement rates of the final environment state across these eight runs.
We evaluated GPT-4 and Claude as agents.

We ran conformance tests confirming that each tool behaves as documented. Two tools are simulated stubs that return fixed placeholder responses; this is disclosed in the paper and also stated in the tool descriptions shown to the agent.
The grader takes the final environment state as its input. We validated the grader on 150 injected correct and incorrect outcomes, finding a false-accept rate of 1% and a false-reject rate of 2%.

Web access is blocked during runs; retrieval is confined to the task environment, preventing answer leakage through search. A private held-out test split with concealed labels is excluded from all public surfaces. Released tasks include a canary string.
